rows.original: ahiṃsan sarvabhūtāny anyatra tīrthebhyaḥ (Sanskrit not seen on a listed site)
rows.translation: F. Max Müller, SBE 1 (1879)
rows.says: The Upanishad ends by describing the householder who studies the Veda, brings up virtuous sons and pupils, draws his senses into the Self and never gives pain to any creature except at the tīrthas. Whoever lives so all his life reaches the world of Brahman and does not return.
rows.bearing: A Tier 1 wider duty not to harm any creature (sarvabhūtāni). It reaches every person K1 protects, newborns and outsiders included (rules 7 and 9), so it teaches K1 and K0 through the wider rule. The exception 'except at the tīrthas' is glossed in Müller's text as '(sacrifices, &c.)', and his footnote reports the commentator (not named in the search result) as saying that even a wandering mendicant causes pain, but may importune people for alms at tīrthas, or sacred places; others explain it differently. Neither reading reaches a private person killing a person. Śaṅkara's own words on the verse were not seen.

rows.original: ahiṃsā satyam akrodhas tyāgaḥ śāntir apaiśunam / dayā bhūteṣv aloluptvaṃ (16.2); tejaḥ kṣamā dhṛtiḥ śaucam adroho nātimānitā (16.3)
rows.translation: Swami Gambirananda (Advaita Ashrama), checked against Swami Sivananda, with the Sanskrit. sources/translations.md names K. T. Telang (SBE 8), which is not in the local data and was not seen
rows.says: The marks of one born to the divine nature include non-injury, truthfulness, absence of anger, kindness to creatures and non-covetousness (16.2), and forgiveness and freedom from malice (16.3). The divine nature leads to liberation, the demonic to bondage (16.5). Śaṅkara glosses non-injury as not causing pain to living beings, and absence of anger as calming the anger that arises when one is reviled or struck by others. Rāmānuja and Śrīdhara gloss non-injury as avoiding pain to others.
rows.bearing: A Tier 1 wider duty of non-injury and kindness to all creatures, reaching everyone K1 protects (rule 7). It is taught as a character to cultivate, so it is Clear teaching, not Explicit. Absence of anger, freedom from malice (adroha) and non-covetousness bear directly on K0's motives, and Śaṅkara's gloss (not answering abuse or blows with anger) bears on revenge. The same book's call to fight is war (rule 5).
rows.strength: Clear teaching (wider rule for K1; direct for K0's motives)

rows.translation: Swami Gambirananda (Advaita Ashrama), checked against Swami Sivananda, with the Sanskrit. sources/translations.md names K. T. Telang (SBE 8), which is not in the local data and was not seen
rows.says: Those of demonic nature are 'giving themselves wholly to passion and anger' and seek wealth 'through foul means' (16.12). They say: 'I have slain that enemy, and I shall slay others too. I am the Lord, the Enjoyer' (16.14). Resorting to egotism, power, arrogance, passion and anger, they hate God in their own and others' bodies (16.18). They fall into a foul hell (16.16), and God casts these hateful, cruel, vilest of people into demonic births (16.19).
rows.bearing: Killing one's enemies out of desire, anger, pride and enmity, and gaining wealth by unjust means, are given as the outlook of the nature to be shunned and bound for ruin. This teaches K0 (no killing for gain, or out of anger, hatred or revenge) at Clear teaching level. 16.19 is God consigning the cruel to lower births, not a human killing, so it gives no permission to anyone (rule 4). On its own the passage does not reach K1's whole wording (rule 7); K1 rests on the wider-rule rows.

rows.reference: Bhagavad Gita 17.19 (= Mahabharata critical ed. 6.39.19), with Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja and Śrīdhara Svāmin on the verse; read with 14.18
rows.original: mūḍhagrāheṇātmano yat pīḍayā kriyate tapaḥ / parasyotsādanārthaṃ vā tat tāmasam udāhṛtam; Śrīdhara: anyasya vināśārtham abhicārarūpam
rows.translation: Swami Gambirananda (Advaita Ashrama), checked against Swami Sivananda, with the Sanskrit. sources/translations.md names K. T. Telang (SBE 8), which is not in the local data and was not seen. Commentaries read in Sanskrit; English paraphrase is the verifier's
rows.says: Austerity done from a foolish notion, by torturing oneself, or 'for the destruction of others', is of the dark quality, tamas. Those of the tamas quality go down (14.18). Śaṅkara glosses 'for the ruin or destruction of another'; Rāmānuja the same; Śrīdhara says it is austerity 'for the destruction of another, in the form of abhicāra' (hostile sorcery).
rows.bearing: A counted text that classes spiritual practice aimed at destroying another person as of the lowest kind, and a classical commentator who applies it to hostile sorcery. This is the tradition's own narrowing, within Tier 1, of the sorcery texts (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12, the Atharvaveda rites, the śyena). It does not cancel them: it speaks of austerity (tapas), not of offerings or curses, and it grades rather than forbids in so many words. Under rule 6 it is a narrowing reading, which is why the hard cases give Unclear rather than Contradicted. It also shows that the tradition treats such practices as real acts against another.
rows.strength: Clear teaching (that practice aimed at destroying another is of the lowest quality)

rows.says: Rāmānuja explains that the Self cannot be killed, and adds that scriptural rules such as 'do not harm any creature' and 'a brahmin must not be killed' concern causing a body's separation from its self where scripture has not enjoined it.
rows.bearing: A second classical authority, besides Śaṅkara on Brahma Sūtra 3.1.25, who treats 'do not harm any creature' as binding scripture with exceptions only where scripture itself enjoins a killing (here, a warrior's lawful battle). That keeps the Gita's metaphysical verses from becoming a licence, and confines the exceptions to scripture's own settings (war, sacrifice, punishment: exclusions a, b and e). It would not on its own settle hostile rites, since the Mīmāṃsā debate is over whether Vedic sorcery is 'enjoined' as right (Śabara row, unverified).

rows.reference: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.12 (Müller, SBE 15, VI, 4, 12; Hume (1921) appended on the next sacred-texts page)
rows.original: yasya jāyāyai jāraḥ syāt taṃ ced dviṣyāt (as recalled; the Sanskrit was not seen)
rows.translation: F. Max Müller, SBE 15 (1884); R. E. Hume (1921) for the opening
rows.says: If a man's wife has a lover and he hates him, he is to put fire in an unbaked (unannealed) vessel, lay out reed arrows in reverse order, and make offerings in which he takes away the lover's sons, cattle, sacred works and hopes. 'He whom a Brâhmaṇa who knows this curses, departs from this world without strength and without good works.' The passage ends by warning men not to desire the wife of a learned brahmin who knows this rite.
rows.bearing: A Tier 1 text, accepted by all branches, in the same section as 6.4.7, which the households annex counts against Hinduism. It prescribes, in injunctive form, a rite that a husband performs on his own authority because he hates a man who threatens no one's life, and whose stated outcome is that the man 'departs from this world' stripped of strength and merit. If the rite is a deliberate killing, it is private, out of hatred, and not defence, so it would bear directly against K0 (hatred) and K1 (a husband's private act). Three points are unresolved. (1) Whether killing by rite or curse is 'deliberately killing' in K1 and K0: a question for every tradition (for example curses such as 2 Kings 2:23 to 24). (2) Whether 'departs from this world' here means that the rite kills him, or that he will die, whenever he dies, without strength and merit. The phrase usually means dying, but no classical commentary on this verse was seen (Śaṅkara's was searched for and not found). (3) The tradition's own narrowing: Gita 17.19 (read directly) classes practice 'for the destruction of others' as tamasic, and Śrīdhara applies it to hostile sorcery; Manu 9.290 fines such rites; Mīmāṃsā holds that hostile rites are not right conduct (unverified). Under rule 6 the result is Unclear for K1 and K0. It would be Contradicted if the project counts killing by rite as killing, reads the verse as causing death, and gives no weight to the narrowing.

rows.reference: Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 7.13 to 18 (pañcikā 7, adhyāya 3; Haug's 'VII, 3'): the story of Śunaḥśepa
rows.translation: M. Haug (1863) or A. B. Keith, HOS 25 (1920); neither seen. The narrative was seen only as summarised by J. Eggeling (introduction to SBE 44) and in a wisdomlib study
rows.says: King Hariścandra has vowed his son to the god Varuṇa. The son buys the boy Śunaḥśepa from his starving father Ajīgarta for a hundred cows, as a substitute. When no one else will, Ajīgarta binds the boy and takes up the knife to kill him for more cows. The boy prays to the gods and is freed. Viśvāmitra condemns Ajīgarta's deed, the boy rejects his father, and Viśvāmitra adopts him.
rows.bearing: Two sides. The story condemns a father who would kill his child for gain, which supports K0 and K1's protection of children. But its frame has a god demanding a human sacrifice and accepting a substitute, and a king who intends to give his son. The killing is never carried out and the would-be killer is condemned (rule 4). The god's acceptance of a victim makes it a hard case. It is a ritual killing, not a judicial punishment, so exclusion (a) would not obviously cover it. If verified at the primary-text level, the likely result is Implied for support and, at most, Unclear (rule 6) as counter-evidence.

It neither commands nor approves a killing, so it is Implied (rule 4). A reader who took it as a licence would make it at most Unclear (rule 6), which would not change K1, already Unclear. rows.says: The Self neither kills nor is killed (2.19); it is not killed when the body is killed (2.20); how can one who knows it kill, or cause anyone to be killed (2.21)? One free of the sense of 'I', whose understanding is untainted, does not kill and is not bound, even if he kills these creatures (18.17). Śaṅkara says 18.17 is praise (stuti) and explains it by two standpoints, the worldly one (he kills) and the ultimate one (he does not). On 2.21 he says the verse's point is that the knower is free of all action, killing being given only as an example. K1.label: Unclear (rule 6)
K1.reason: Without the hard case, K1 would be Taught (wider rule) in counted texts that all four main branches accept. Gita 16.2, 13.7 and 17.14 (Tier 1, Clear teaching, read directly) teach non-injury towards all beings, and Śaṅkara glosses it as not causing pain to living beings. Chāndogya 8.15.1 (Tier 1, Explicit, VERIFIED by search) says the same. Its exception 'except at the tīrthas' is read as sacrifices (Müller) or as a mendicant begging at sacred places (Müller's commentator), and neither reading reaches the killing of a person. These teachings reach newborns and outsiders (rules 7 and 9). One counted text bears directly on K1 and is unresolved: Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12 (Tier 1, all branches; VERIFIED by search on sacred-texts.com; not available locally, so not read directly). It tells a husband who hates his wife's lover, acting on his own authority, to perform a rite against that man, who threatens no one's life. The text says that the man whom a brahmin who knows this curses 'departs from this world without strength and without good works'. Three points remain open. (1) It is a project-wide question whether killing by rite or curse counts as 'deliberately killing', and the same rule must then apply to curses in other traditions. (2) It is not settled whether the phrase means that the rite kills him; no classical commentary on the verse was seen. (3) The tradition's own counted text narrows such practice: Gita 17.19 (read directly) classes austerity aimed at 'the destruction of others' as tamasic, the lowest quality, and Śrīdhara applies it to hostile sorcery. Manusmṛti 9.290 (Tier 2, weakly verified) fines such rites. So rule 6 applies on two grounds: it is a hard case the wording does not plainly cover, and a counted text narrows it. Atharvaveda 10.1 (search) is a second rite of the same kind, but on the hymn's own terms it falls within the defence exception. Other hard texts do not decide. Kauṣītaki 3.1 (search) and Gita 2.19 to 21 and 18.17 (direct) speak of the knower's state, and Śaṅkara calls 18.17 praise (stuti), so they are Implied (rule 4). Gita 4.8 is God's own action (Implied). Śatapatha 13.6.2.13 releases its human victims. Manusmṛti 11.31 to 33 is Tier 2 and contested. The unverified Tier 1 leads (the śyena, the Atharvaveda petitions, Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.5.10.3, Śunaḥśepa) would at most also be Unclear. What would change the label: if the project rules that killing by rite or curse is not 'deliberately killing', or that the verse does not describe a death, K1 becomes Taught (wider rule). If it rules that such rites are killings, reads the verse as causing death, and holds that Gita 17.19 does not reach a Vedic injunction, the label becomes Contradicted (rule 2: a private killing out of hatred, in all branches). It would then be the Hindu counterpart of Numbers 35:26 to 27, Phinehas or Abū Dāwūd 4361, and should be labelled the same way those are. Those texts describe killing by physical means, so the means question does not arise for them. The Hindu case also has a counted narrowing text (Gita 17.19), which plays the role a classical narrowing plays elsewhere. No branch split: every deciding row is a Tier 1 text that all four main denominations accept.

K0.label: Unclear (rule 6)
K0.reason: K0 is taught directly at Clear teaching level in Tier 1 texts read directly. Gita 16.2 to 3 lists absence of anger, non-covetousness and freedom from malice as divine marks, and Śaṅkara glosses absence of anger as calming the anger that arises when one is reviled or struck, which bears on revenge. Gita 16.12 to 19 gives 'I have slain that enemy, and I shall slay others too', said by those given over to passion and anger who seek wealth by foul means, as the outlook bound for ruin. Gita 16.21 says passion, anger and greed are the three gates to hell and must be given up (Explicit for the motives). Gita 12.13 and 11.55 teach hatred of no creature and enmity towards no being. K0 is also taught through the wider-rule rows used for K1. The same Tier 1 hard case decides K0 too, and bears on it even more directly: Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12 (search) names hatred as the husband's motive (taṃ ced dviṣyāt), and the rite is not defence. The three open points are the same as for K1: whether killing by rite counts, whether the curse kills, and the narrowing by Gita 17.19 (direct, with Śrīdhara on abhicāra). So the label is Unclear (rule 6). The Atharvaveda refrain against 'him whom we hate' is unverified and is a petition (rule 4, Implied). Manusmṛti 11.31 to 33 (retaliation by spell) is Tier 2 and does not decide. Manusmṛti 4.164 (no striking in anger) supports K0 but is Tier 2. Alternatives as for K1: K0 is Taught if killing by rite is ruled out of the wording, and Contradicted (all branches) if it is counted and the narrowing is given no weight.

K3.label: Silent in counted texts
K3.reason: The Tier 1 war texts, read directly, say nothing on non-combatants. Gita 1.36 and 2.31 to 38 call a warrior to a righteous battle between armies and do not say who may be killed in it. Gita 11.33 to 34 name only enemy warriors. The wider rule of non-injury (Gita 16.2) does not count for K3 on its own, because the same text sets righteous war apart without saying how far its permission reaches. Whether non-injury still protects non-combatants in war is therefore a matter of argument (Implied). This matches the annex's treatment of wider duties where the texts themselves accept the practice. The Ṛg Veda hymns on Indra's wars are a god's deeds and petitions to him (rules 4 and 5) and are unverified. The Atharvaveda battle charms were not checked, so the silence is only moderately established. Tier 2, not counted (rule 1): Manusmṛti 7.91 to 93 (VERIFIED by search on sacred-texts.com) explicitly forbids striking those who surrender ('I am thine'), supplicants, sleepers, the unarmed, the naked, onlookers, the wounded, the frightened and those who flee. It does not name children, women or the old. Āpastamba 2.5.10.11, Baudhāyana's rule sparing women, infants and the old, the Mahabharata's agreed battle rules and the Sauptika Parva's condemnation of a night massacre remain unverified. Under the tier rule these developed rules of fair war do not count, and the article should say so plainly.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The narrowing (ground 3) is both misdescribed and understated. Misdescribed: Gita 17.19 grades austerity (tapas). A fire offering such as Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12 ('juhuyāt') falls under the Gita's grading of sacrifice (17.11 to 13, read directly, verse ids 606 to 608). There, an offering made according to injunction but aimed at a result is rājasa (17.12), not tāmasa, and tāmasa sacrifice is the one 'contrary to injunction' (vidhihīnam, 17.13). So 17.19 alone does not plainly reach this rite. Understated: the classical commentators in the local gita/gita dataset (commentary.json, read directly in this check) narrow Vedic hostile rites expressly, across schools. (1) Madhusūdana Sarasvatī on 2.32 (verse id 79): 'śyenādayo hi vihitā api phaladoṣeṇa duṣṭāḥ': the śyena and similar rites, though enjoined, are faulty because their result, the killing of an enemy (śatruvadha), is forbidden by 'na hiṃsyāt sarvā bhūtāni' and 'brāhmaṇaṃ na hanyāt' and brings sin (pratyavāya), and there is no injunction on the result (phale vidhyabhāvāt). (2) The same on 18.7 (id 630), in his own conclusion: 'vihitaśyenaphalasyāpi śatruvadharūpasyābhicārasya anarthahetutvam upapadyata eva' (the hostile rite whose result is killing an enemy is a cause of harm, even though the śyena is enjoined). He also says the general prohibition covers harm rooted in passion and hatred. (3) The same on 3.36 (id 155) lists 'śatruvadhasādhanaṃ ca śyenādi' among the sinful acts a deluded person does. (4) Nīlakaṇṭha on 1.38 (id 38): 'nahi vidhimātrād yatkiṃcit kartavyam; śyenādīnām adharmarūpāṇām apy avaśyānuṣṭheyatvāpatteḥ' (nothing is to be done merely because it is enjoined; otherwise the śyena and the like, which are adharma, would have to be done). (5) Dhanapati on 5.3 (id 207) calls the śyena and the hostile rites (ābhicārika) 'dveṣamūlaka', rooted in hatred. (6) Rāmānuja on 18.28 (id 651) describes the tāmasa agent as 'abhicārādikarmaruciḥ', one who delights in hostile rites and plans lasting harm to others. Vedānta Deśika glosses this as 'tāmasa acts taught in scripture' (śāstrodita). (7) Śaṅkara on 13.2 (dataset 13.3, id 492) gives hostile sorcery (abhicaraṇa) as his example of action driven by faults such as passion. (8) Śrīdhara and Madhusūdana on 17.19 (id 614) gloss the verse as abhicāra, and Abhinavagupta (Kashmir Śaiva) on 17.17 to 19 says tamasic faith is faith in destroying others (parotsādana). The principle that the Śabara row records as UNVERIFIED is therefore attested directly in classical commentators, although Śabara's own words are still not seen. No Dvaita commentary on 17.19 exists in the dataset: Madhva and Jayatīrtha did not comment on it.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 6 (a reading that the tradition's own counted texts or classical commentators narrow); METHOD.md section 3, 'No cherry-picking' (show the tradition's own reconciliation, citing its authorities); METHOD.md section 9, decision 12 (the Gita with its classical commentaries counts as VERIFIED (direct)).
objections.proposed: Keep Unclear (rule 6), but rest ground (3) on Gita 17.19 together with the commentators listed. Say that 17.19 by itself speaks of austerity, and that on the Gita's own grading of sacrifice (17.12) an enjoined offering made for a result is rājasa. Add a reconciliation row: VERIFIED (direct, gita/gita): commentary.json, Madhusūdana on ids 79, 155, 630 and 641; Nīlakaṇṭha on id 38; Dhanapati on id 207; Rāmānuja and Vedānta Deśika on id 651; Śaṅkara on id 492; link https://bhagavadgita.io/chapter/2/verse/32/. Mark the Śabara row's principle as verified (direct) in later classical commentators, with Śabara's own locus and words still UNVERIFIED. Correct the 17.19 bearing ('it grades rather than forbids in so many words'): Madhusūdana states outright that the hostile rite's result is forbidden and brings sin.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Ground (1), whether killing by rite counts as 'deliberately killing', is treated as open. For Hinduism, the tradition's own classical commentators settle it. They call the result of the hostile rite 'śatruvadha', the performer's killing of an enemy, and place it under 'na hiṃsyāt' as the performer's sin (Madhusūdana on 2.32, 3.36 and 18.7, read directly). Abhinavagupta on 18.4 reports the Mīmāṃsaka view that sacrificial killing is not hiṃsā but 'the śyena and the like are hiṃsā'. Manusmṛti 11.33 ('slay his enemies') and 9.290 (Tier 2) point the same way. The row's comparison with 2 Kings 2:23 to 24 does not fit. There God answers the curse (divine action, rule 4), as with the Atharvaveda petitions, which the rows rightly rate Implied. Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12 is a technique the performer works himself ('I take away your ...'). The tradition counts such a technique as his own act.
objections.rule_basis: Brief section 2.2 (texts, read with the tradition's own reconciliation, are the test); rule 4 (petitions and divine action are Implied) as the line for parity; rule 6 (it needs an unresolved meaning, not a question the tradition answers).
objections.proposed: Drop ground (1) as a ground for Unclear. Keep it only as a project-wide note on the wording, with this parity line: curses answered by God are divine action (rule 4), and rite techniques the tradition itself counts as the performer's killing are the performer's act. Remove or qualify the 'Taught if killing by rite is ruled out' alternative: that ruling would override the tradition's own understanding.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Ground (2), whether 'departs from this world' means the rite kills, is the researcher's own doubt. No reading within the tradition has been found that disputes it. The row itself concedes that 'asmāl lokāt praiti' usually means dying. Rule 6 asks for a disputed word or an unresolved reach, not merely an unconsulted commentary. For parity: Stoicism's De Ira 1.15.2 was labelled Contradicted although an alternative reading was noted, while Zoroastrianism's Unclear rested on documented disagreement between translators. The row also records, from memory, a breath formula in the rite (taking the man's in-breath and out-breath) that the search did not show. If that clause is confirmed, ground (2) closes as 'a death'.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 6 (disputed word or unresolved reach); consistency with the Stoicism (De Ira 1.15.2) and Zoroastrianism (Yasna 31.18, 33.2) labels.
objections.proposed: Do not count ground (2) as an independent rule 6 ground. Record it as a Textual gap with a concrete next step: confirm Müller's or Hume's wording of the breath formula in 6.4.12, and find Śaṅkara's bhāṣya on the verse (Mādhavānanda's translation). The label stays Unclear on ground (3) alone.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The stated alternatives and the parity claim do not hold. (a) Contradicted route: 'holds that Gita 17.19 does not reach a Vedic injunction' is not enough. The commentators apply the prohibition expressly to enjoined hostile rites. So Contradicted would need the project to set aside a classical narrowing, which it did not do for Mahāyāna Buddhism (Mahāparinirvāṇa narrowed by the same sūtra: Unclear) or for Christianity (Numbers 35:27 narrowed by Romans 12:19 to 13:4 and Aquinas: Unclear). (b) The claim that the case 'should be labelled the same way' as Numbers 35:26 to 27, Phinehas or Abū Dāwūd 4361 cannot be applied, because those are labelled differently from one another. Judaism: provisionally Contradicted. Christianity: Unclear for the same verse. Sunni Islam: Contradicted in one branch, where the commentators widen rather than narrow. The principle these labels actually follow is: a counted narrowing gives Unclear; no narrowing, or a widening, gives Contradicted. (c) The Taught route is fragile. Madhusūdana on 18.7 quotes 'śyenenābhicaran yajeta' as a Vedic injunction for hostile sorcery. Its Tier 1 source (the Ṣaḍviṃśa Brāhmaṇa lead) is still UNVERIFIED and decides nothing (rule 1), but once verified it would bring back the same Unclear even if 6.4.12 were read as non-lethal.
objections.rule_basis: Rules 1, 2 and 6; METHOD.md section 9, decision 7 (later authorities never outweigh a contradicting counted text) and decision 8 (narrowing never gives Taught on its own); cross-tradition consistency.
objections.proposed: Rewrite 'What would change the label'. Taught only if 6.4.12 is shown not to describe a death and no other verified Tier 1 hostile rite (such as the śyena) stands. Contradicted only if the project decides that classical commentators' narrowing does not count under rule 6, and that decision must then also apply to Mahāyāna Buddhism and Christianity. Replace the parity sentence with the narrowing-versus-widening principle.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Strongest case for Contradicted, considered and rejected. The tradition's own verified rule ranks remembered texts (smṛti) below revealed ones (śruti) (Śaṅkara on Brahma Sūtra 2.1.1, search). The Gita sits inside the Mahabharata, which decision 4 treats as smṛti. Śaṅkara on Brahma Sūtra 3.1.25 and Rāmānuja on Gita 2.19 (read directly) also hold that a specific scriptural injunction overrides the general ban on harm. On this argument the Gita cannot narrow an Upaniṣadic injunction, and the verified classical rules favour the injunction. It fails because the commentators do not set the Gita against the Upaniṣad. They read the Vedic injunction as covering only the means for someone who already wants the harm, with no injunction on the result (Madhusūdana on 2.32, 'phale vidhyabhāvāt'). The death is then not 'enjoined' in the sense of Rāmānuja's own clause (avihita), so the general prohibition, which they treat as śruti, applies. The narrowing therefore works inside śruti's own reading.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 6; METHOD.md section 3, 'No cherry-picking' (show both sides and the tradition's own reconciliation).
objections.proposed: Keep Unclear. State this objection and its answer briefly in the reason, so readers can see why the tradition's ranking of texts does not undo the narrowing.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Strongest case for Taught, considered and rejected. Every classical commentator found who discusses hostile rites calls them sinful or tāmasa, and under rule 2 'a sin before God' is not permission. So, the argument runs, the tradition reads 6.4.12 as not permitting the killing. It fails because the counted text itself, on its face, prescribes the rite to a private person out of hatred. Its sinfulness comes from later authorities and from a counted text (Gita 17.19) about a different practice. Decision 7 says later authorities never outweigh a contradicting counted text, and decision 8 and rule 6 say narrowing gives Unclear, never Taught.

objections.label: K1

Glossing Arjuna's objection at Gita 1.36 (verse id 36, read directly), Śrīdhara, Nīlakaṇṭha and Dhanapati quote the six kinds of ātatāyin and the licence 'ātatāyinam āyāntaṃ hanyād evāvicārayan'. They then rank it as arthaśāstra, weaker than the dharmaśāstra rule 'na hiṃsyāt sarvā bhūtāni', citing Yājñavalkya. Śrīdhara: 'arthaśāstraṃ dharmaśāstrād durbalam'. Purushottamji attributes the verses to Manu 8.350. The caveat is that this explains Arjuna's view, which Kṛṣṇa overrides on war grounds.
objections.rule_basis: METHOD.md section 3, 'No cherry-picking' (record the tradition's reconciliation).
objections.proposed: Add this as reconciliation beside the ātatāyin rows: VERIFIED (direct, gita/gita) for the commentators' words, while the Tier 2 law-book references stay as they are. No label effect, because those rows are Tier 2.

objections.proposed: Keep it as context within the defence exception, and say openly that if the project does not accept that, it is a second rule 6 hard case. It cannot be a contradiction while the commentators' narrowing of hostile rites stands.

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: The narrowing bears on K0 even more directly than the reason shows. Gita 3.34 (Tier 1, all branches, verse id 153, read directly in this check: 'tayor na vaśam āgacchet', 'One should not be swayed by these two', meaning attraction and aversion, rāga and dveṣa) is an Explicit counted instruction against acting from aversion. It is missing from the rows. Among the commentators, Dhanapati on 5.3 calls hostile rites 'rooted in hatred'. Madhusūdana on 18.7 applies the general prohibition to harm rooted in passion and hatred, and on 6.32 (id 265) names hatred as what produces the killing of enemies ('śatruvadhādikaro dveṣaḥ'). The condition in Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12, 'taṃ ced dviṣyāt' (if he hates him), is exactly what these address. Grounds (1) and (2) fall away for K0 for the same reasons as for K1.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 6; rule 7 (Explicit and Clear teaching count); METHOD.md section 9, decision 12.
objections.proposed: Keep Unclear (rule 6). Decision 7 bars Taught while 6.4.12 stands. Add a support row for Gita 3.34 (Explicit for not acting under the sway of aversion; Clear teaching for K0's hatred clause; link https://bhagavadgita.io/chapter/3/verse/34/). Cite the commentators as the narrowing.

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: Gita 16.14 ('I have slain that enemy') condemns the demonic outlook as a whole, mainly egotism ('I am the Lord, the Enjoyer'). Read alone, it is a description of a type rather than a rule on motive. Its value for K0 comes from 16.12 ('given wholly to passion and anger', wealth 'by foul means') and from 16.21.
objections.proposed: Keep Clear teaching, but say that the motive clause rests on 16.12 and 16.21.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: The reason deals only with Gita 16.2. Chāndogya 8.15.1, rated Explicit (wider rule) in the rows, has no war exception in its own text: its only exception is the tīrthas. By parity with Buddhism, where K3 was labelled Taught (wider rule) partly because Dhp 129 to 130 has no war exception, one could argue K3 is Taught here too. The answer is that Buddhism's K3 rested on SN 42.3, a war text that condemns killing in battle as such. Hinduism's counted war texts do the opposite: Gita 2.31 to 38 calls the warrior to righteous battle. Its commentators read the general prohibition as yielding there: Rāmānuja on 2.19 (read directly in the rows), and Madhusūdana on 2.32 (read directly in this check), who says war's result is not forbidden, unlike the śyena's. Neither says how far that suspension reaches. The annex analogy in the reason ('where the texts themselves accept the practice') is also loose. The counted texts accept war, not the killing of non-combatants. The real point is that they suspend the wider rule for righteous war without fixing its limits.
objections.rule_basis: Rules 6, 7 and 8; METHOD.md section 3, 'Wider rules' (the wider rule must reach everyone); consistency with Buddhism (Taught via SN 42.3) and Stoicism (verified wider rule, K3 Silent).
objections.proposed: Keep 'Silent in counted texts', with Chāndogya 8.15.1 addressed alongside Gita 16.2 and the annex analogy restated as above. Record the alternative: Unclear (rule 6), if the project treats a wider rule that the same texts suspend for war, without stated limits, as a counted text whose reach is unresolved. Parity with Stoicism favours Silent.

K1.label: Unclear (rule 6)
K1.reason: Baseline: Taught (wider rule). Gita 16.2, 13.7 and 17.14 (Tier 1, all branches, Clear teaching, read directly, with Śaṅkara's gloss 'not causing pain to living beings') and Chāndogya 8.15.1 (Tier 1, VERIFIED (search); better rated Clear teaching) teach non-injury towards every being, which reaches newborns and outsiders (rules 7 and 9). Rāmānuja on 2.19 (read directly) keeps 'na hiṃsyāt sarvā bhūtāni' binding on every killing that scripture has not enjoined. One counted text accepted by all four main denominations bears directly: Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12 (Tier 1, VERIFIED (search) on sacred-texts.com). It tells a husband who hates his wife's lover, a man attacking no one, to perform a rite on his own authority, and says the man such a brahmin curses 'departs from this world without strength and without good works'. On its face that permits a private killing, out of hatred, of someone who is not attacking (rules 2 and 5). The tradition narrows it. Its counted text, Gita 17.19 (read directly), classes practice 'for the destruction of others' as tamasic, the quality that 'goes down' (14.18). Its classical commentators, read directly in the gita/gita dataset, hold that Vedic hostile rites, though enjoined, are sinful because their result, the killing of an enemy, falls under 'na hiṃsyāt sarvā bhūtāni': Madhusūdana on 2.32, 3.36 and 18.7; Nīlakaṇṭha on 1.38 ('adharma'); Dhanapati on 5.3 ('rooted in hatred'); Rāmānuja and Vedānta Deśika on 18.28 (tāmasa); Śaṅkara on 13.2 (driven by faults); Śrīdhara on 17.19. This is a narrowing by counted texts and classical commentators, so the label is Unclear (rule 6), not Contradicted. Decision 7 bars Taught while the text stands. The 'is a rite a killing?' question is not a separate ground: the tradition itself counts the result of such rites as the performer's killing (śatruvadha, hiṃsā). One textual gap remains: whether 6.4.12 describes a death. The idiom suggests it does, and a breath formula is recalled but not seen. The next step is to confirm that wording and read Śaṅkara's bhāṣya on the verse. What would change the label: Taught only if 6.4.12 is shown not to describe a death and no other verified Tier 1 hostile rite stands (the śyena injunction, quoted as Vedic by Madhusūdana on 18.7, is unverified at source). Contradicted only if the project rules that classical narrowing does not count under rule 6, a ruling that would also change Mahāyāna Buddhism and Christianity. Other hard texts do not decide. Kauṣītaki 3.1 and Gita 2.19 to 21 and 18.17 are about the knower's state (Implied; Śaṅkara calls 18.17 praise). Gita 4.8 is God's action (Implied). Śatapatha 13.6.2.13 releases its victims. Atharvaveda 10.1 is defence on its own terms. Manusmṛti 11.31 to 33 is Tier 2 and contested. No split among the four main denominations, since Gita 17.19 narrows for all. Whether the Arya Samaj is a branch (decision 3) is undecided.

K0.label: Unclear (rule 6)
K0.reason: K0 is taught directly in Tier 1 texts read directly, all branches. Gita 16.2 to 3 (absence of anger, freedom from malice, non-covetousness; Śaṅkara: calming the anger that arises when one is reviled or struck) and 16.12 to 19 (killing enemies from passion and anger, and wealth by foul means, as the outlook bound for ruin) are Clear teaching. Gita 16.21 (give up passion, anger and greed) is Explicit for the motives. Gita 3.34 ('One should not be swayed by' attraction and aversion), Explicit for not acting from aversion, should be added to the rows. Gita 12.13 and 11.55 (hate no creature, no enmity towards any being) are Clear teaching. The same Tier 1 hard case bears on K0 more directly than on K1. Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12 (VERIFIED (search)) makes hatred the condition of the rite ('taṃ ced dviṣyāt'), and the rite answers a wrong, not an attack. The narrowing is also more direct. Counted texts forbid acting from aversion (3.34, 12.13) and class practice aimed at destroying others as tamasic (17.19). Classical commentators, read directly, call hostile rites 'rooted in hatred' (Dhanapati on 5.3), apply the prohibition of harm to harm rooted in passion and hatred (Madhusūdana on 18.7), and name hatred as what produces the killing of enemies (Madhusūdana on 6.32). Rule 6 gives Unclear, and decision 7 bars Taught while the counted text stands. Manusmṛti 4.164 (no striking in anger) supports but is Tier 2. Manusmṛti 11.31 to 33 is Tier 2 and contested. The Atharvaveda refrain against 'him whom we hate' is an unverified petition (rule 4). Alternatives as for K1: Taught only if 6.4.12 does not describe a death and no other verified hostile rite stands; Contradicted only if classical narrowing is ruled not to count.

K3.label: Silent in counted texts
K3.reason: The Tier 1 war texts, read directly, say nothing on non-combatants. Gita 1.36 and 2.31 to 38 call a warrior to a righteous battle between armies, and 11.33 to 34 name only enemy warriors. The wider duty of non-injury (Gita 16.2; Chāndogya 8.15.1, which has no war exception in its own text) does not count for K3 on its own. The tradition's counted texts set righteous war apart (2.31 to 38), and its commentators read the general prohibition as yielding there: Rāmānuja on 2.19, and Madhusūdana on 2.32, who says war's result is not forbidden, unlike the śyena's. They do not say whether that suspension reaches people who are not fighting. So any protection of non-combatants by the wider rule is a matter of argument (Implied). This differs from Buddhism, whose K3 rests on SN 42.3, a war text that condemns killing in battle as such. It matches Stoicism, where a verified wider rule left K3 Silent. The Ṛg Veda hymns on Indra's wars are a god's deeds and petitions (rules 4 and 5) and are unverified. The Atharvaveda battle charms were not checked, so the silence is only moderately established. Tier 2, not counted (rule 1): Manusmṛti 7.91 to 93 (VERIFIED (search)) explicitly forbids striking those who surrender, supplicants, sleepers, the unarmed, onlookers, the wounded, the frightened and those who flee. It does not name children, women or the old. Āpastamba, Baudhāyana and the Mahabharata's battle rules and Sauptika Parva remain unverified. The article should say plainly that these developed rules of fair war are real but do not count under the tier rule. Alternative: Unclear (rule 6), if the project treats a wider rule suspended for war without stated limits as a counted text whose reach is unresolved.

challenge.consistency_notes: The principle the other traditions' labels actually follow is this. Where a counted text approves a private killing and nothing in the tradition narrows it, or its authorities widen it, the label is Contradicted. That covers Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2 in Stoicism; Abū Dāwūd 4361 in Sunni Islam, where the commentators widen; and Numbers 35:26 to 27 in Judaism, provisionally, where no narrowing was accepted. Where the tradition's own counted texts or classical commentators narrow the text, the label is Unclear. That covers the same Numbers verse in Christianity, narrowed by Romans 12:19 to 13:4 and Aquinas; Phinehas; and the Mahāparinirvāṇa in Mahāyāna Buddhism, narrowed by the same sūtra. Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12 belongs in the second group. Its narrowing comes from a counted text (Gita 17.19, plus 3.34 for K0) and from several classical commentators across Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita and Kashmir Śaiva lines. They address Vedic hostile rites expressly and call them sinful despite the injunction. This narrowing is stronger and more specific than Christianity's for Numbers 35:27, so Unclear for K1 and K0 is consistent. The proposed sentence saying the case 'should be labelled the same way' as Numbers 35, Phinehas or Abū Dāwūd 4361 should be replaced, because those texts carry different labels in different traditions. The project lead may also want to check whether Judaism's provisional Contradicted on Numbers 35:27 considered a narrowing by counted texts (for example Proverbs 24:29); on Christianity's reasoning it might also be Unclear. On the means question, parity should follow rule 4. Curses or petitions that God answers (the Atharvaveda petitions; 2 Kings 2:23 to 24; imprecatory psalms) are divine action and Implied. A rite technique that the tradition itself counts as the performer's killing (as Madhusūdana does for the śyena) is the performer's act, and the Hindu rows should not treat it as an open question. Zoroastrianism's Unclear rested on documented disagreement between translators (Yasna 31.18 and 33.2). The Hindu doubt over whether 'departs from this world' describes a death is not documented in that way, so it should not ground Unclear on its own. That matches Stoicism, where an undocumented alternative reading did not prevent Contradicted. For K3, Silent matches Stoicism and Zoroastrianism. It differs from Buddhism because Buddhism has a war text (SN 42.3) condemning killing in battle, while Hinduism's war texts suspend the wider rule without stating limits.
